{"id": "20:135/q09", "question": "What does 'the level path' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the path is explained as a road, religion, justice, or its destination.", "positions": [{"id": "20:135/q09/p1", "position": "It is the straight, upright way or road without deviation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya glosses ṣirāṭ as road; al-Biqāʿī adds broad, clear, unbending and fit for reaching one's aim; al-Bursawī calls it balanced. Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ call it a straight road."}, {"id": "20:135/q09/p2", "position": "It is the upright or true religion, specifically Islam in al-Suddī's gloss.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās as reported by al-Wāḥidī calls it upright religion; Yaḥyā reports al-Suddī's Islam gloss; al-Jishumī, al-Ṭabrisī and Ibn al-Jawzī identify true religion."}, {"id": "20:135/q09/p3", "position": "It is justice or the just way.", "reasons": "Muqātil gives justice; al-Suddī as reported by al-Durr does likewise; Yaḥyā reports al-Suddī's just religion. Al-Qurṭubī reports al-Zamakhsharī's justice gloss for sawāʾ."}, {"id": "20:135/q09/p4", "position": "It is the road to Paradise or everlasting bliss.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā describes the just road to Paradise; al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī offer this as Judgment Day sense; al-Nasafī says everlasting bliss."}]}
{"id": "20:135/q10", "question": "How is the consonant of ṣirāṭ recited?", "turns_on": "Whether the consonant is pronounced with sīn or with ṣād shaded toward zāy.", "positions": [{"id": "20:135/q10/p1", "position": "The sīn pronunciation is a canonical dialectal reading.", "reasons": "Qirāʾāt ER calls sīn etymologically original and ṣād an emphatic Qurayshī adaptation."}, {"id": "20:135/q10/p2", "position": "Ishmām shades ṣād toward zāy.", "reasons": "Qirāʾāt ER describes a sound intermediate between ṣād and sīn."}]}
{"id": "20:135/q11", "question": "How is al-sawiyy read, and what do the variants signify?", "turns_on": "The transmitted vowels, hamza and feminine or diminutive morphology determine whether the adjective means level, middle, or bad.", "positions": [{"id": "20:135/q11/p1", "position": "The usual al-sawiyy means straight or level.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn call it majority or general reading on faʿīl; al-Ālūsī gives the straight gloss."}, {"id": "20:135/q11/p2", "position": "Al-sawāʾ or al-siwāʾ means the middle, best, just, or even path.", "reasons": "Abū Mijlaz and ʿImrān ibn Ḥudayr are named by Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, and al-Ālūsī; al-Qurṭubī cites al-Zamakhsharī's middle, justice and upright glosses. The notes differ in vowel transcription."}, {"id": "20:135/q11/p3", "position": "Al-sūʾ or al-sūʾā makes the path bad or evil, contrasting it with the guided person.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is reported with al-sūʾ; Ibn Yaʿmar and al-Jaḥdarī with the feminine form, which treats ṣirāṭ as feminine. Al-Qurṭubī notes 1:6 uses masculine. Al-Naḥḥās defends the unhamzated form by substitution; Abū Ḥātim challenges its derivation."}, {"id": "20:135/q11/p4", "position": "A diminutive variant derives from sawāʾ, the even or middle way.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and the Shaykh prefer this origin, comparing ʿaṭāʾ to ʿaṭiyy; they object that a diminutive of sūʾ should retain hamza. Al-Samīn also discusses a reversed yāʾ-to-wāw change in the doubled-wāw form."}, {"id": "20:135/q11/p5", "position": "A diminutive variant derives from sūʾ, the bad way.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī gives this analysis; Abū al-Baqāʾ agrees, and al-Samīn notes hamza replacement is allowed. Abū Ḥayyān and the Shaykh object that hamza should remain."}, {"id": "20:135/q11/p6", "position": "The unhamzated feminine form is morphologically unacceptable.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥātim argues that sūʾ would yield al-sūʾā and sawāʾ another form, transcribed al-siyyā or al-siyy; al-Naḥḥās counters with permitted hamza substitution."}]}
{"id": "20:135/q12", "question": "How is the second man connected grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the second man is interrogative or relative, and, if relative, which prior constituent it coordinates with.", "positions": [{"id": "20:135/q12/p1", "position": "It is another interrogative nominative subject with an implied predicate, parallel to the first question.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says the resumptive is omitted; al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī treat both clauses as the content of knowing. Al-Naḥḥās says it coordinates with the first man."}, {"id": "20:135/q12/p2", "position": "It is a relative nominative pronoun coordinated with the first clause or its subject.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī allow coordination with the suspended question or subject; al-Samīn cites Abū al-Baqāʾ that this coordinates a declarative with an interrogative. Al-Ālūsī requires ʿalima to mean recognition if an object would otherwise be omitted."}, {"id": "20:135/q12/p3", "position": "It coordinates with aṣḥāb, describing the one who is guided.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī list this alternative; al-Ālūsī says both descriptions can belong to the Prophet."}, {"id": "20:135/q12/p4", "position": "It is genitive by coordination with ṣirāṭ, meaning the path of the guided one.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives the path of those who followed guidance; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī allow ṣirāṭ to mean the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "20:135/q13", "question": "What does 'was guided' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase states guidance simply or stresses its achieved benefit.", "positions": [{"id": "20:135/q13/p1", "position": "It means being rightly directed, reaching truth, or escaping error.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya glosses right direction; Ibn Kathīr adds reaching truth; al-Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī specify guidance out of error."}, {"id": "20:135/q13/p2", "position": "It means attaining guidance's benefit and avoiding harm, beyond merely possessing a path.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī distinguishes possession from actual knowledge and use of the path."}]}
{"id": "20:135/q14", "question": "Why pair 'people of the path' with 'who was guided'?", "turns_on": "Whether the pairing distinguishes prior error, the use of a path, or the contrast created by a variant reading.", "positions": [{"id": "20:135/q14/p1", "position": "The first can name those who never strayed; the second those who strayed then found guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ gives this distinction; al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī transmit it."}, {"id": "20:135/q14/p2", "position": "Possessing the path differs from attaining and benefiting from its guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says possession alone does not ensure knowledge or use; the second expression asks who gained benefit and avoided harm."}, {"id": "20:135/q14/p3", "position": "On the negative-path readings, the second clause explicitly contrasts evil with guidance.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the variant divides the parties; Abū Ḥayyān says this contrast is explicit unlike the majority reading; al-Ālūsī says comparison is absent in the usual and first anomalous readings."}]}
{"id": "20:135/q15", "question": "How does the final warning address its audience?", "turns_on": "Whether the notes explain its address and ellipsis or its threatening force.", "positions": [{"id": "20:135/q15/p1", "position": "The final warning shifts to direct address and omits a parallel clause made clear by context.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī contrasts it with the indirect address in 20:133–134 and takes the shift as heightened anger."}, {"id": "20:135/q15/p2", "position": "The closing statement is a severe threat, warning, and intimidation.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī and al-Qurṭubī identify its force; Ibn Kathīr compares 25:42 and 54:26; al-Rāzī says it rebukes without implying doubt."}]}
{"id": "20:135/q16", "question": "Was the command to wait abrogated?", "turns_on": "Whether the appeal to 9:5 establishes abrogation; Ibn al-Jawzī denies it.", "positions": [{"id": "20:135/q16/p1", "position": "An unnamed view says the sword verse, conventionally 9:5, abrogated it.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī reports the claim only to reject it as baseless."}, {"id": "20:135/q16/p2", "position": "The abrogation claim is baseless.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī explicitly rejects the unnamed claim."}]}
{"id": "20:135/q17", "question": "What inward path does the ending describe?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:135/q17/p1", "position": "The guided reach God through spiritual stations and detachment from everything else; attachment to other things cuts people off.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī gives this inward reading; Khujandī's couplet says union begins with separation from all else."}]}
{"id": "20:135/q18", "question": "What does respite leave people accountable for?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:135/q18/p1", "position": "God has removed excuses through respite and guidance, so the decisive proof belongs to Him.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī adds a report, citing 17:15, of three who plead excuse: one dying in the interval, a person without reason, and a child; their response to a fire test discloses their standing. Kur'an Yolu says hearers retain freedom of choice until truth becomes clear."}]}
{"id": "20:135/q19", "question": "What duty and patience does this ending leave the Prophet?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:135/q19/p1", "position": "He must warn, worship, and patiently await God's decision while leaving unresponsive people to their choice.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī warns that haste opened Adam to deception, says prayer fosters patience, and says divine provision removes need to court the wealthy. Kur'an Yolu urges steady worship and effort; Iṣlāḥī says a delivered warning benefits willing hearers without making the Prophet answerable for others."}]}

{"id": "20:135/q21", "question": "How does the sūra relate to its setting and the next sūra?", "turns_on": "The notes address different adjacent settings and give no dispute over a single sequence.", "positions": [{"id": "20:135/q21/p1", "position": "The sūra consoles the Prophet amid Makkan insults and ends with a warning after accounts of Moses, Adam, and the Last Day.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites 20:9, 20:97, 20:115 and 20:124; Kur'an Yolu ties the close to pressure and perseverance."}, {"id": "20:135/q21/p2", "position": "It followed Maryam and figures in the account of ʿUmar's conversion.", "reasons": "Study Quran says ʿUmar read a parchment at his sister's house, then went to profess faith; it mentions 19:1."}, {"id": "20:135/q21/p3", "position": "The connection of Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ with the preceding sūra is self-evident.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī states this without further argument."}]}
{"id": "20:135/q22", "question": "What reports promise a virtue for reciting this sūra?", "turns_on": "Which of two reported rewards or recitations is described.", "positions": [{"id": "20:135/q22/p1", "position": "A reciter of Ṭā Hā receives the Resurrection reward of the Emigrants and Helpers.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf reports this from the Prophet without grading; al-Bayḍāwī repeats it."}, {"id": "20:135/q22/p2", "position": "The people of Paradise recite no Qur'an except Ṭā Hā and Yā Sīn.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf and al-Nasafī report this from the Prophet without grading; al-Bursawī transmits it from al-Kashshāf."}]}
{"id": "20:135/q23", "question": "What makes a literary resemblance or attribution apt?", "turns_on": "Whether an attributed likeness follows an actual, graspable relation.", "positions": [{"id": "20:135/q23/p1", "position": "A genuine analogy requires intelligible resemblance and fitting proportions, not merely a simile marker or borrowed word.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī says forced likeness is awkward; discovering hidden rational similarity resembles finding a pearl, while a composite object's parts must fit its form and proportions."}, {"id": "20:135/q23/p2", "position": "A skilled imitator may be called a learner following a predecessor, so a craft may be attributed to that predecessor.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī gives this as an example of accurate imitation and attribution."}]}
{"id": "21:32/q01", "question": "What does جعلنا mean in this construction?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:32/q01/p1", "position": "It can express creation even with two objects.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashi says Arabic جعل with one object means create, while with two it can mean create, name, or transform; the two-object form alone does not establish creation."}]}
{"id": "21:32/q02", "question": "What does السماء designate here?", "turns_on": "Whether the sky is read cosmically or as an inward faculty.", "positions": [{"id": "21:32/q02/p1", "position": "The visible heaven above earth, including celestial space.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu understands the protected roof as both Earth's atmosphere and cosmic space containing galaxies, solar systems and stars formed from the nebula's fragmentation; Asad calls it a secure canopy."}, {"id": "21:32/q02/p2", "position": "The rational faculty in an inward reading.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani reads the raised, protected sky as reason, guarded from change, forgetfulness and error, while people ignore its proofs."}]}
{"id": "21:32/q03", "question": "Why is the sky singular?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:32/q03/p1", "position": "The singular is generic and evokes the one roof visible to people.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i says most people observe only the lowest heaven; one protected roof also conveys its preservation."}]}
{"id": "21:32/q04", "question": "Why call the sky سقفا, a roof?", "turns_on": "Whether the image emphasizes its raised roof shape or the wave imagery in transmitted descriptions.", "positions": [{"id": "21:32/q04/p1", "position": "It arches or stands over the earth as a house roof stands over a house.", "reasons": "Mujahid and al-Tabari call it raised. Al-Wahidi cites 52:5 and the house analogy; al-Razi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Bursawi, al-Biqa'i and the Study Quran likewise use roof or canopy comparisons. Abu Hayyan says anything raised and arched over something is a roof. Ibn Ashur specifies a roof laid on house walls, as a direct simile, and cites the absence of pillars in 13:2. Ibn Kathir describes a dome, citing 51:47, 91:5 and 50:6, and compares Arab tent construction and the Prophet's 'Islam built on five' image. Al-Biqa'i adds that this roof contains light, guidance signs and ornaments. Asad compares 13:2."}, {"id": "21:32/q04/p2", "position": "It is a restrained wave.", "reasons": "Qatada calls it a restrained or contained wave; transmitted wording varies. A reported Prophetic description likewise calls it a restrained wave running like an arrow."}]}
{"id": "21:32/q05", "question": "Why is سقفا singular if the skies are plural?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:32/q05/p1", "position": "The heavens together form one roof over earth.", "reasons": "Al-Farra' compares them with a house roof."}]}
{"id": "21:32/q06", "question": "What does محفوظا grammatically modify?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:32/q06/p1", "position": "The masculine participle modifies سقف; a feminine form could instead modify السماء.", "reasons": "Al-Farra' compares the masculine/feminine variation تغشى/يغشى in 3:154; al-Nahhas states both agreement possibilities. Al-Jishumi adds that the later 'its signs' refers to the sky."}]}
{"id": "21:32/q07", "question": "In what sense is the roof protected?", "turns_on": "Which threat or quality 'protected' specifies: devils, falling, deterioration, human reach, moral defilement, or general/cosmic security; al-Razi also disputes the means of guarding against devils.", "positions": [{"id": "21:32/q07/p1", "position": "It is guarded from devils and their eavesdropping by stars or shooting meteors.", "reasons": "Muqatil says devils cannot overhear angels and relay it to people. Yahya, Ibn Abbas via al-Wahidi and Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi, al-Jubba'i, and others cite 15:17 or 37:6–7. Al-Tabari calls them rejected devils. Al-Tabataba'i prefers this sense. Al-Alusi objects that the roof image then seems idle; the reply compares thieves climbing earthly roofs. Al-Razi favors angels instead, reasoning that stars need not stop harm from stolen hearing."}, {"id": "21:32/q07/p2", "position": "God keeps it from falling upon earth, despite lacking supporting pillars.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj and al-Wahidi specify 'except by God's permission'; al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi cite 22:65. Al-Razi also cites 30:25, 35:41 and 2:255; al-Tabrisi cites 35:41. Al-Kashshaf adds quaking. Ibn Ashur stresses the blessing: celestial bodies or their parts do not fall and destroy people or land."}, {"id": "21:32/q07/p3", "position": "It remains intact, free from decay, collapse, corruption or alteration until its appointed end.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi contrasts ordinary roofs' long-term deterioration; al-Hasan says no breach, decay or collapse. Qatada says time does not alter it; al-Alusi says this accords with eventual folding at Resurrection. Al-Baydawi and al-Bursawi qualify the preservation as lasting until the appointed time. Elmalili cites 35:41. Islahi calls it ancient, flawless, free of fissures and cites 50:6, 67:2–4, 17:99 and 79:27–33."}, {"id": "21:32/q07/p4", "position": "Its height keeps it beyond human reach, breach, demolition and other harms.", "reasons": "Mujahid glosses 'protected' as 'raised'; al-Wahidi explains that height keeps demolition and artifice from reaching it. Al-Hasan mentions attempted breach. Ibn Kathir says guarded against being reached. Ibn Atiyya takes preservation broadly, from devils, projectiles and other harms; al-Qurtubi lists human devices and breach."}, {"id": "21:32/q07/p5", "position": "Angels guard it from devils.", "reasons": "Al-Razi reports both angel and star accounts and prefers angels because this magnifies divine guardianship and stars need not prevent damage from jinn stealing a hearing."}, {"id": "21:32/q07/p6", "position": "It is protected from idolatry and sins.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan transmit this sense. Al-Alusi rejects it, invoking his objection to a prior interpretation."}, {"id": "21:32/q07/p7", "position": "It is protected from those below it, thereby protecting them from it.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this further interpretation and says it implies complete safety for people beneath the sky."}, {"id": "21:32/q07/p8", "position": "Its ordered cosmic system is secured by centrifugal force and mutual gravitational attraction.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu describes space as created in divine order and balance, relates this to the preservation of heaven and earth in 35:41, and identifies atmosphere and cosmic space as the protected roof."}, {"id": "21:32/q07/p9", "position": "Its preservation is general rather than limited to one danger.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya includes devils, projectiles and other harms. Al-Biqa'i combines divine prevention of falling with meteor protection from devils; Asad calls it a well-secured canopy."}]}

 "What reports describe the roof as a restrained wave?", "turns_on": "Whether the description is Qatada's report or the report attributed to the Prophet; its chain and force as an explanation are disputed.", "positions": [{"id": "21:32/q08/p1", "position": "Qatada calls it a protected raised roof and a restrained or contained wave.", "reasons": "Yahya's wording is 'protected roof and restrained wave'; al-Tabari's is 'raised roof and contained wave.'"}, {"id": "21:32/q08/p2", "position": "A report through Ibn Abbas attributes a raised, restrained, moving roof protected from devils to the Prophet.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says this directly explains the verse if sound. {"id": "21:32/q09", "question": "Who are وهم?", "turns_on": "Whether the third-person plural singles out unbelievers or describes the wider heedless audience.", "positions": [{"id": "21:32/q09/p1", "position": "The polytheists or unbelievers, especially the Meccan unbelievers.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi reports Ibn Abbas's identification; Ibn al-Jawzi specifies Meccans. Al-Tabari says polytheists, while al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and the Study Quran say unbelievers or idolaters."}, {"id": "21:32/q09/p2", "position": "People generally who are heedless of the signs.", "reasons": "Yahya speaks of people who see without reflecting; al-Biqa'i says most people, while al-Alusi calls them heedless and Islahi says their eyes are shut."}]}
{"id": "21:32/q10", "question": "What are the sky's signs?", "turns_on": "Whether the signs are named heavenly bodies, a wider range of phenomena, or the sky taken together as one sign.", "positions": [{"id": "21:32/q10/p1", "position": "The sun, moon and stars, including other celestial bodies and their motions.", "reasons": "Mujahid and many later transmitters give sun, moon and stars; al-Qurtubi reports Mujahid as sun and moon. Al-Kashshaf adds courses, risings and settings; al-Razi adds directions, conjunctions and separations. Abu Hayyan includes timed motions; Ibn Kathir mentions fixed and wandering stars and the sun's immense circuit. Al-Razi connects their orbits and seasonal effects to day, night and benefits."}, {"id": "21:32/q10/p2", "position": "The signs also include weather and all visible or investigated conditions of the sky.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya lists rain, thunder, lightning and thunderbolts; Ibn Ashur adds clouds, lightning and thunder. Al-Biqa'i includes winds and rains. Al-Baydawi says some conditions are sensed and others studied in natural philosophy and astronomy; al-Kashshaf and Abu Hayyan describe ordered heavenly motions."}, {"id": "21:32/q10/p3", "position": "The sky as a created whole, or any thing in it, is itself a sign.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj says a coordinated set can count as one āya because it points to oneness. Singular-reading explanations by al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, Ibn al-Jawzi, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and al-Alusi variously treat heaven and its contents as one sign, any part as sufficient, or singular as a generic collective. Al-Tabrisi emphasizes signs of createdness and dependence."}]}
{"id": "21:32/q11", "question": "How is آياتها read and understood?", "turns_on": "Whether the word is plural or singular; the singular can name the whole sky or serve as a generic collective.", "positions": [{"id": "21:32/q11/p1", "position": "The plural آياتها names the sky's many signs.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says most reciters read the plural. Al-Farra' says both singular and plural readings are valid; the many bodies and phenomena described by the commentators fit the plural."}, {"id": "21:32/q11/p2", "position": "Mujahid and Humayd read singular آيتها, as one collective or generic sign.", "reasons": "Al-Farra' and Ibn al-Jawzi say the sky and its contents make one sign. Al-Zajjaj calls the sky the greatest sign and says a collection may be one āya. Al-Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi and al-Samin allow a generic collective; al-Alusi says each thing suffices to prove a Creator."}]}
{"id": "21:32/q12", "question": "Why are the signs attributed to the sky?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:32/q12/p1", "position": "They are located in it, though God is their maker.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi contrasts their attribution here to heaven with their attribution elsewhere to God."}]}
{"id": "21:32/q13", "question": "How does the closing clause function grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether وهم begins a new sentence or gives a circumstantial state.", "positions": [{"id": "21:32/q13/p1", "position": "It is a new sentence.", "reasons": "Al-Samin says a prospective circumstantial analysis is weak."}, {"id": "21:32/q13/p2", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur analyzes it as describing the state accompanying God's making the sky. Al-Samin judges a prospective circumstantial reading weak."}]}
{"id": "21:32/q14", "question": "What does turning away from the signs involve, and what should they show?", "turns_on": "Whether the failure is general lack of reflection, selective attention to worldly use, or a spiritual failure to remember God.", "positions": [{"id": "21:32/q14/p1", "position": "People fail to contemplate the signs that prove one Creator's existence, power, wisdom and exclusive divinity.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Tabari, al-Wahidi and al-Qurtubi stress monotheism; Yahya adds belief in the return, invoking 10:101. Al-Baydawi and al-Alusi include divine knowledge, will and wisdom; al-Tabrisi stresses createdness and dependence. Ibn Kathir cites 12:105. Al-Biqa'i says the signs prove resurrection. Islahi calls shut eyes the reason signs do not benefit, and Kur'an Yolu stresses God's power to recreate."}, {"id": "21:32/q14/p2", "position": "They use the sky's worldly benefits while overlooking its proof of the Creator.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf names light, navigation and life-sustaining rain; Abu Hayyan reports his explanation. {"id": "21:33/q01", "question": "What does God's creation of these signs establish?", "turns_on": "Whether the signs establish God's sole agency or prophetic foreknowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "21:33/q01/p1", "position": "God alone creates and governs these signs, proving His power, wisdom, sole divinity and beneficence.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari relates alternation to livelihood and the hereafter; Bursevi says creation from nonexistence proves power; Ibn Ashur says the definite clause excludes idols. {"id": "21:33/q02", "question": "Why does this verse say 'created'?", "turns_on": "How khalaqa relates to jaʿala in the preceding verse.", "positions": [{"id": "21:33/q02/p1", "position": "It concerns creation of the entities themselves rather than their being made in a state.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur contrasts the previous wording."}, {"id": "21:33/q02/p2", "position": "Night and day are unlike substantial creatures, explaining 'created' rather than 'made'.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this and finds it unconvincing."}]}
{"id": "21:33/q03", "question": "What are night and day and what do they do?", "turns_on": "Physical light and shadow versus temporal periods.", "positions": [{"id": "21:33/q03/p1", "position": "Night is darkness and rest; day is light and the time for activity.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir adds their alternating length; Bursevi and Ibn Ashur identify night with Earth's shadow and day with sunlight on its illuminated hemisphere; Kuranyolu stresses benefit to living beings. {"id": "21:33/q04", "question": "Why does night precede day?", "turns_on": "Convention or temporal priority.", "positions": [{"id": "21:33/q04/p1", "position": "Arabic convention puts night first, including Qur'anic phrases and dating by nights.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan cites 2:164, 34:33, 30:17 and notes day is masculine."}, {"id": "21:33/q04/p2", "position": "Darkness or night was created first.", "reasons": "Al-Samarrai compares jinn before humans (15:27), drowsiness before sleep, and cites 24:44 and 6:1."}]}
{"id": "21:33/q05", "question": "Why do sun and moon follow day and appear in that order?", "turns_on": "Natural origin, temporal order or exemplary signs.", "positions": [{"id": "21:33/q05/p1", "position": "Their order points to daylight's origin and to creation or spatial priority.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says sunlight produces day and the moon relieves darkness; al-Burhan places location before time; al-Samarrai says sun existed before moon."}, {"id": "21:33/q05/p2", "position": "They are the greatest signs of day and night, implying other stars.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi says naming them implies the rest; al-Alusi connects the preceding signs and a shift of address."}]}
{"id": "21:33/q06", "question": "What benefits come from the sun and moon?", "turns_on": "Different accounts of the beneficial motion.", "positions": [{"id": "21:33/q06/p1", "position": "They give light, timekeeping, heat and seasonal benefit.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi cites 17:12 for months, years and reckoning; Ibn Kathir distinguishes their lights, paths and measures; Bursevi mentions heat and cold; Kuranyolu notes reflected moonlight."}, {"id": "21:33/q06/p2", "position": "Their measured latitude and timing spread effects without destructive extremes.", "reasons": "Razi says north-south inclination and paced cycles prevent permanent severe seasons; intellect grasps only a little."}, {"id": "21:33/q06/p3", "position": "The sun comes closer in winter and rises in summer for welfare.", "reasons": "Al-Aʿmash says the changes help and prevent heat injury."}]}
{"id": "21:33/q07", "question": "How does the verse connect to the surrounding signs?", "turns_on": "Surrounding signs, opponents' demand, or parallel verses.", "positions": [{"id": "21:33/q07/p1", "position": "It expands prior sky signs into sun, moon, day and night as gifts.", "reasons": "Razi says it answers neglect of heavenly signs; Baydawi calls it further explanation; Alusi points to 21:32; Study Quran points to 36:40 and cosmological discussion."}, {"id": "21:33/q07/p2", "position": "The signs answer opponents' demand for proof and warn against celestial worship.", "reasons": "Islahi connects the challenge to 21:8 and says the bodies' obedience makes another sign needless."}, {"id": "21:33/q07/p3", "position": "It parallels other accounts of calculated celestial motion.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir cites 36:40 and 6:96; Study Quran directs readers to 36:40."}]}
{"id": "21:33/q08", "question": "Who or what does 'each' include?", "turns_on": "Whether the nearby two suffice or plural and context expand the set.", "positions": [{"id": "21:33/q08/p1", "position": "The sun and moon are the immediate referents.", "reasons": "Al-Samin prefers them because night and day do not swim; Islahi says kull can gather two nouns; Nasafi treats them as classes; Bursevi takes each separately."}, {"id": "21:33/q08/p2", "position": "It includes night, day, sun and moon.", "reasons": "Al-Samin and Abu al-Baqa allow all four; Qurtubi adds stars and planets; Biqai and Tabatabai give the four courses, the latter night as a conical shadow; Asad says all float in space."}, {"id": "21:33/q08/p3", "position": "It includes sun, moon and unnamed stars or all rising bodies.", "reasons": "Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Razi infer stars from the plural; Tabrisi includes them because night is named; Elmalılı supplies an omitted conjunct; Ibn Ashur calls them sky signs. Al-Alusi also records stars as a referent and calls night-and-day inclusion unsuitable because they do not swim."}, {"id": "21:33/q08/p4", "position": "Sun and moon are generic classes embracing many bodies or risings.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari and Baydawi cite successive risings; Elmalılı prefers encompassing all stars, some moon-like; Nasafi calls them classes."}, {"id": "21:33/q08/p5", "position": "Previously mentioned Earth joins sun and moon.", "reasons": "Elmalılı reports the possibility that every body has its own orbit."}]}
{"id": "21:33/q09", "question": "What does the tanwin of 'each' signify?", "turns_on": "What is omitted and whether tanwin compensates.", "positions": [{"id": "21:33/q09/p1", "position": "It replaces an omitted genitive complement, 'each of them'.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi and Ibn Ashur explain; al-Burhan cites 2:253 and 30:4 for this rare omission."}, {"id": "21:33/q09/p2", "position": "The complement is singular indefinite, 'each one'.", "reasons": "Alusi reports Zamakhshari; Ibn Hisham says the pronoun should then be singular; Abu Hayyan allows either agreement."}, {"id": "21:33/q09/p3", "position": "The complement is plural definite, as the agreement shows.", "reasons": "Ibn Hisham derives it from the plural verb."}, {"id": "21:33/q09/p4", "position": "The tanwin may be ordinary declension.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan reports this alternative to substitution."}]}
{"id": "21:33/q10", "question": "How is 'in an orbit, they swim' parsed?", "turns_on": "Predicate choice and sentence attachment.", "positions": [{"id": "21:33/q10/p1", "position": "Kull is subject and yasbahun predicate; fi falak attaches to the verb.", "reasons": "Al-Samin and Abu al-Baqa invoke agreement by sense; Baydawi and Alusi allow the parsing."}, {"id": "21:33/q10/p2", "position": "Kull is subject, fi falak predicate and yasbahun circumstantial.", "reasons": "Al-Samin, Abu al-Baqa, Bursevi, Alusi and Ibn Ashur take the locative as predicate; Alusi cites distributive singular falak."}, {"id": "21:33/q10/p3", "position": "The whole kull sentence is circumstantial of sun and moon.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari, Baydawi, Nasafi and al-Samin allow accusative; the Shaykh excludes night and day because they do not swim."}, {"id": "21:33/q10/p4", "position": "The whole sentence is an independent resumption.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and al-Alusi allow no syntactic slot."}]}

{"id": "21:33/q14", "question": "Where is the orbit and how many spheres are proposed?", "turns_on": "Location and counting depend on differing physical schemes and reports.", "positions": [{"id": "21:33/q14/p1", "position": "The orbit lies between heaven and Earth or below the sky.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd cites 25:61; Awf describes a dome and unfastened bodies, Jerusalem twelve miles from heaven and al-Ubulla farthest; Hasan says attachment would prevent running."}, {"id": "21:33/q14/p2", "position": "Seven planetary spheres have further stellar or enclosing levels.", "reasons": "Wahidi reports seven planetary spheres; Qurtubi prefers seven below heavens and names zodiac and greatest as eighth and ninth; Alusi reports seven plus fixed-star and daily-motion spheres."}, {"id": "21:33/q14/p3", "position": "There may be fewer or more than nine, with extra nested levels.", "reasons": "Alusi reports eight- and seven-sphere schemes, Avicenna's doubt about fixed stars, hidden motion differences such as Herschel's, and epicycles and lunar node spheres; similar movements do not prove one sphere."}, {"id": "21:33/q14/p4", "position": "A planet's sphere may sit inside each heaven, with intervals described by reports.", "reasons": "Alusi prefers sound 500-year reports; allows an internal mover, fixed stars above the heavens or within seventh, doubts many cosmological reports and disputes astronomical distances."}, {"id": "21:33/q14/p5", "position": "All stars may lie in the lowest heaven.", "reasons": "Alusi says separate deferent-like spheres fit 37:6."}, {"id": "21:33/q14/p6", "position": "The sun is in the fifth heaven in winter and seventh in summer.", "reasons": "Ibn Amr says it could not stay in the apparent lowest heaven."}, {"id": "21:33/q14/p7", "position": "Sun and moon face heaven and turn their backs toward Earth, lighting both.", "reasons": "Ibn Amr cites 71:15–16."}]}

{"id": "21:33/q16", "question": "Do stars move intrinsically, with spheres, or both?", "turns_on": "Intrinsic versus carried movement.", "positions": [{"id": "21:33/q16/p1", "position": "Stars move themselves through resting spheres or courses.", "reasons": "Razi and Bursevi's Imam favor this apparent fish-in-water reading; Alusi says the verse suggests travel within sphere thickness yet is ambiguous about rest; Elmalılı says old carrier astronomy is overturned; Abu Sulayman has motion without the sphere rotating the stars."}, {"id": "21:33/q16/p2", "position": "Moving spheres carry stationary embedded stars.", "reasons": "Philosophers reject independent travel as rupturing solid spheres; Bursevi likens signet and ring; Alusi challenges the proof and exclusivity."}, {"id": "21:33/q16/p3", "position": "Sphere and star can both move, same or opposed, at equal or differing speeds.", "reasons": "Razi, Ibn al-Shaykh and Alusi list the models as possible."}, {"id": "21:33/q16/p4", "position": "A separate small ring or hollow track could carry a planet.", "reasons": "Alusi allows a ring as wide as the planet, or a hollow course in moving or resting sphere, admitting a vacuum against Aristotle."}, {"id": "21:33/q16/p5", "position": "Stars might be suspended from chains of light moved by angels.", "reasons": "Alusi doubts this report but affirms divine power."}, {"id": "21:33/q16/p6", "position": "The orbit itself may be assigned the running.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports this grammatical alternative."}]}

Razi and Bursevi say this does not prove rationality."}, {"id": "21:33/q22/p2", "position": "It includes unnamed stars with sun and moon.", "reasons": "Jishumi and Razi infer more than two; Abu Hayyan supplies a conjunct; Samin cites other verses."}, {"id": "21:33/q22/p3", "position": "Sun and moon denote repeated risings or classes.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari and Baydawi give the successive-risings explanation; Elmalılı prefers inclusion of all stars, some moon-like."}, {"id": "21:33/q22/p4", "position": "It follows the sense of kull or grammatical predominance.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa says each swimming entails all swimming; Biqai says predominance; Burhan objects to making each individual plural."}, {"id": "21:33/q22/p5", "position": "The form suits the verse ending.", "reasons": "Kisai cites 54:44; Samin mentions cadence. Al-Alusi records honorific precedence as another rationale."}, {"id": "21:33/q22/p6", "position": "The bodies really are rational beings.", "reasons": "Avicenna argues from this form and Joseph's dream (12:4); Alusi reports some Muslims; Razi and Bursevi answer with personification."}]}
{"id": "21:33/q23", "question": "Are the celestial movers rational or living?", "turns_on": "Literal grammatical inference and nature of movers.", "positions": [{"id": "21:33/q23/p1", "position": "Planets or spheres are living rational beings.", "reasons": "Avicenna infers from agreement and 12:4; philosophers describe spheres as living, knowing and volitional; theologians object."}, {"id": "21:33/q23/p2", "position": "Agreement does not prove literal rationality.", "reasons": "Razi and Bursevi cite personification; Bursevi invokes 27:18 and considers speech to proceed from the heart rather than tongue, mentioning angels, jinn and parrots."}, {"id": "21:33/q23/p3", "position": "Immaterial rational souls move the celestial bodies.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports spiritual thinkers who distinguish movers from matter while linking them to spheres."}]}
{"id": "21:33/q24", "question": "What did a Friday creation report say?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:33/q24/p1", "position": "God created night and day during two of Friday's hours.", "reasons": "Al-Durr reports a reply to Jews asking the Prophet about Friday."}]}
{"id": "21:33/q25", "question": "What wordplay occurs in kull fi falak?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:33/q25/p1", "position": "It reads identically forward and backward, an even palindrome.", "reasons": "Itqan gives 74:3 as the other Qur'anic example; Ibn Ashur notes seven letters and Sakkaki's term al-maqlub al-mustawi."}]}
{"id": "21:33/q26", "question": "What inward meanings are assigned to the signs?", "turns_on": "Distinct spiritual correspondences.", "positions": [{"id": "21:33/q26/p1", "position": "Night and day are soul and intellect, lit by spirit and heart, ascending toward God.", "reasons": "Qashani gives spiritual ranks and stations."}, {"id": "21:33/q26/p2", "position": "Night and day are the gnostic's contraction and expansion.", "reasons": "Kashifi links majesty to contraction and beauty and generosity to expansion."}, {"id": "21:33/q26/p3", "position": "Sun is stable divine-unity realization; moon is waxing and waning states.", "reasons": "Kashifi contrasts a fixed witnessing presence with changing states between loss and full realization."}]}
{"id": "21:33/q27", "question": "How should cosmological claims be weighed?", "turns_on": "Authority of reports, apparent wording and observation.", "positions": [{"id": "21:33/q27/p1", "position": "Stay with sound reports and avoid unwarranted precision.", "reasons": "Tabari refuses a shape without scripture or report; Razi requires transmission; Alusi says early generations had little practical reason to describe cosmology and doubts many reports; Study Quran attributes revelation-based caution to Qurtubi and Razi."}, {"id": "21:33/q27/p2", "position": "Observation supports a sphere and allows reports to be interpreted.", "reasons": "Ghazali sides with sensory evidence and reads 21:33 as suggesting circularity without explicit flatness."}, {"id": "21:33/q27/p3", "position": "Scripture should guide reconciliation of scientific theories.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says science should be reconciled with Qur'an when they seem to conflict."}, {"id": "21:33/q27/p4", "position": "Astronomical schemes remain possible but not exclusively proved.", "reasons": "Alusi questions numbers, distances and motion details, citing modern London and Ibn Arabi alternatives."}]}
{"id": "21:33/q28", "question": "How is sabaha related to tasbih in Arab usage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:33/q28/p1", "position": "Tasbih means declaring God free of evil, prayer, or wonder; swimming and running are related terms.", "reasons": "Jishumi cites poetry on Alqama's boast for subhana and records the wonder reading."}]}
{"id": "21:66/q01", "question": "Had the people understood Abraham's proof when he spoke?", "turns_on": "Whether the evident proof had actually been grasped by the people; al-Razi cites Abraham's subsequent questions for the second possibility.", "positions": [{"id": "21:66/q01/p1", "position": "They had already recognized that his argument was sound.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari presents this as one possible timing after the failed excuse and the truth's disclosure."}, {"id": "21:66/q01/p2", "position": "The proof was apparent, but they had not understood it.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari gives this alternative; al-Razi favors it because Abraham still asks about their worship and reasoning."}]}
{"id": "21:66/q02", "question": "What force does the opening af convey?", "turns_on": "The notes give different glosses for af: an expression of annoyance or a word for filth and stench.", "positions": [{"id": "21:66/q02/p1", "position": "It voices Abraham's annoyance and displeasure.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari calls af an uttered sound of annoyance: Abraham was exasperated that they persisted in worship after their excuse failed and the truth became clear."}, {"id": "21:66/q02/p2", "position": "It signifies filth or stinking, directed at them and their idols.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi gives this gloss alongside Abraham's cutting off their argument."}]}
